_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla, typed out on the slip. Each lesson has two: "start" comes on as the lesson opens, and "check" is a short quiz once the lesson's check is done. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies" (none means a plain "Roger. Over."). A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. Tonight’s question sounds easy and isn’t: how high is that cloud? No balloon, no aeroplane. Just your eyes, four words of Latin, and, believe it or not, your hands.

replies.back: Four words of it, and friendly ones.

turns.them: The three floors of the sky, how the names are built, and three quick tricks. Questions at the end.
Harrow, Walla Walla. Quiz. A lumpy layer of cloud on the middle floor. Build its name.

replies.back: Alto- for the middle floor, cumulus for the lumps. You’re speaking Latin now.
That’s a smooth, high veil. The middle floor is alto-, and lumps are cumulus: altocumulus.
Close, but that’s the low lumpy sheet. The middle floor takes alto-: altocumulus.

turns.them: A layer of lumps high in the sky, and each lump is wider than three fingers held at arm’s length. Which floor?

replies.back: Right. Big lumps are close lumps. Wider than three fingers, it’s low.
Altocumulus lumps sit between a little fingernail and three fingers. Wider than three fingers is the low floor: stratocumulus.
Cirrocumulus grains are smaller than your little fingernail. Wider than three fingers is low: stratocumulus.

turns.them: Soft, feathery wisps up high, with no shading at all. What are they made of?

replies.back: Right. Ice evaporates slowly, so the edges go soft and fibrous.
Droplets make crisp edges. Soft, feathery ones are ice: cirrus.
Smoke drifts low and brown. Feathery white wisps up high are ice: cirrus.

turns.them: Every floor called. Next lesson, the high clouds that tell tomorrow’s weather.
